Justice Stevens mentioned several factors justifying this methodology. 
For one, he noted, “the regulatory scheme is technical and complex, the 
agency considered the matter in a detailed and reasoned fashion, and the 
decision involves reconciling conflicting policies.” For another, he 
mentioned that “[jjudges are not experts in the field, and are not part of 
either political branch of the Government.” By contrast, he claimed that 
“[wjhile agencies are not directly accountable to the people, the Chief 
Executive is, and it is entirely appropriate for this political branch of the 
Government to make such policy choices.” Federal judges had “no 
constituency” and, thus, had “a duty to respect legitimate policy choices 
made by those who do.”
Although parts of Chevron suggest an attempt to establish a simplified 
approach to deference, it is not clear that the Chevron Court itself intended 
any significant change to the underlying law on standards of review. See 
Thomas W. Merrill, The Story of Chevron.* The Making of an Accidental 
Landmark, 66 Ad min . L. Re v . 253, 275-76 (2014). Three justices 
(Marshall, Rehnquist, and O’Connor) did not participate in the 
consideration of Chevron, leaving the Court with only six justices to decide 
the case. It seems doubtful that the Court intended a major statement in a 
case in which a third of its members did not participate. And three years 
after the Chevron decision. Justice Stevens authored a majority opinion in 
another case that seemed not to embrace a broad reading of Chevron. See 
INS V. Cardoza-Fonseca, 480 U.S. 421, 446-48 (1987) (describing the issue 
before the Court as “a pure question of statutory construction for the courts 
to decide”).
Nevertheless, the idea that Chevron embraced a two-step process for 
deferring to agency interpretations took hold. As reflected in the block 
quote above, the first step was “whether Congress has directly spoken to 
the precise question at issue.” If congressional intent was “clear” after 
“employing traditional tools of statutory construction,” a reviewing court 
was required to give that intent effect. But Congress could “explicitly 
[leave] a gap for the agency to fill” through “an express delegation of 
authority,” or it could do so “impHeit[ly].” Where Congress had “not directly 
addressed the precise question at issue,” Chevron instructed that “the court 
does not simply impose its own construction on the statute, as would be 
necessary in the absence of an administrative interpretation.” Rather, the 
second step of Chevron asked “whether the agency’s answer is based on a 
permissible construction of the statute.” In this fashion. Chevron indicated 
that “[t]he court need not conclude that the agency construction was . . . 
even the reading the court would have reached if the question initially had 
arisen in a judicial proceeding.”
